title: Injective Helix 2026: when two IDs became one
summary: Binary-options markets on Injective bound an insurance fund by hashing identity fields end to end. Without separators, two different field tuples collided, a phantom deficit was settled with dust, and about $4.8M left the system. We rebuild the encoding mistake.

case.name: Injective Helix binary options / insurance fund ID collision
case.impact: ~$4.8M across hundreds of short-lived markets (same BlockSec weekly window as Aquifer)

body:
Injective's Helix binary options markets each expected their own insurance fund: a pool meant to cover a deficit when settlement accounting said the market owed more than it held. The link between a market and its fund was an identifier derived from market identity fields. Public analysis (BlockSec, late August 2026) shows that identifier was built by joining variable-length fields end to end and hashing the result — without length prefixes or separators that would preserve structure.

When an encoding is not structure-preserving, two different tuples can produce the same digest. An attacker created markets whose derived fund id collided with a fund that held a different denomination (for example dust INJ bound where USDC was assumed). Settlement then computed a large "deficit" using per-side entry prices that do not cancel under a single oracle price, covered that deficit from the colliding fund without checking denomination, and refunded full margins. Repeated across many short-lived markets with oracles that never posted, the net drain reached roughly $4.8M.

The root class is identifier collision / ambiguous serialization. It is not Solana account confusion and not Aquifer's caller-chosen Token program, but it rhymes: the system trusted a name without proving the name uniquely meant one resource. Fixes use domain-separated or length-prefixed encodings so distinct field tuples cannot map to one id, and payout paths must check denomination as well as amount.

ZKCTF's PDAs are derived from fixed seeds ("config", "round", "entry" + wallet). Those seeds are short constant strings, not concatenated user strings of unknown length — on purpose. Any future feature that hashes user-supplied bytes into an id must add explicit separators.

Reproduction exercise: the Python toy below mirrors the ambiguous join. Which market B parameters collide with market A's fund id?

exercise.statement: fund_id = sha256(quote + base + oracle) hex[:8]. Market A: quote=USDC, base=INJ, oracle=pyth.inj. Attacker keeps oracle=pyth.inj and sets quote=USD. Which base_denom makes the raw concatenation identical to A's? Answer ZKCTF{base_denom}.
artifacts:
import hashlib

def fund_id(quote, base, oracle):
    # VULNERABLE: no separators / length prefixes
    return hashlib.sha256((quote + base + oracle).encode()).hexdigest()[:8]

assert fund_id("USDC", "INJ", "pyth.inj") == fund_id("USD", "???", "pyth.inj")
# A bytes:  USDC + INJ + pyth.inj  →  USDCINJpyth.inj
# B bytes:  USD  + ??? + pyth.inj  →  must equal the same string
hints: Write A's full string with no spaces: USDCINJpyth.inj.
B starts with USD and ends with pyth.inj — what must sit in the middle?
